title: From Accra to Seattle (with a Few Detours)
summary: How managing a print shop in Ghana taught me systems thinking—and why it matters at Salesforce.

content.html:
The Unlikely Tech Education

My first 'production environment' wasn't a server cluster—it was a 10x12 foot print shop in Accra's Makola market. Juggling toner refills, client demands, and a temperamental Heidelberg machine taught me:

  • User Experience: 'The client wants blue, not cyan' translates directly to UI design.
  • Debugging: When the printer jammed, I learned to trace problems upstream (literally—paper path analysis).
  • Load Testing: Market-day rush hour is the analog version of a traffic spike—except the crash comes with yelling.

The Pivot Points

  1. 2009: Taught myself PHP with a dog-eared 'For Dummies' book and XAMPP. First website was a blog for a neighborhood barber.
  2. 2014: Built a church management system that crashed spectacularly during Easter service (my first 'postmortem' involved paper sign-in sheets and 200 mildly disappointed Ghanaians).
  3. 2016: Moved to the U.S., worked night shifts while teaching myself Laravel and React on lunch breaks.
  4. 2022: Shipped a Tableau integration at Salesforce that now processes 2M+ marketing events daily—and requires far fewer duct tape fixes.
"In tech, your past isn't irrelevant—it's your secret advantage. My print shop days made me obsessive about observability."

Lessons for Career Changers

SkillPrint ShopSoftware Engineering
ResourcefulnessMacGyvered paper jamsDebugging legacy Perl at 2AM
Stakeholder MgmtNegotiating with ink suppliersAligning PMs and engineers
ResilienceExplaining to angry customers why their wedding invitations were pink instead of peachExplaining to execs why their Tableau dashboard is missing data
Time ManagementPrint 500 flyers before 5am prayers startShip a hotfix before the marketing team wakes up

The Culture Shift

Coming from Accra's high-stakes small business hustle to the world of tech in the U.S. felt like shifting from survival mode to scale mode. But one thing that stayed constant was systems thinking. Whether it's toner inventory or asynchronous jobs, it's all inputs, outputs, and bottlenecks.

That mindset helped me feel at home in software engineering. I didn't need to pretend I came from a typical background—because mine gave me a kind of edge. I understood real users. I knew what it meant to build under constraints. I’d literally been on fire (small electrical fire, Epson 4800, long story).

From Makola to Meetings

People ask how I made the leap. The truth is, there wasn’t one leap. It was a staircase made of forum posts, bugs I couldn’t fix, bugs I did fix, and an unhealthy number of late-night coding sprints. It was volunteering for that one confusing Jira ticket no one wanted. It was saying "yes" before I felt ready—and Googling like my life depended on it.

Some days, I still feel like the print shop guy who stumbled into a Zoom meeting. But then someone asks me to debug a gnarly issue or mentor a junior dev, and I realize: I belong here. Not in spite of where I came from. Because of it.

Lessons & Reflections

  • Non-traditional paths don’t need justification—they’re often your superpower.
  • Systems are everywhere, and the more you’ve wrestled with them, the better you’ll be at spotting patterns.
  • Success is less about knowing the most and more about staying in the game long enough to figure things out.

This post offered an unexpected lens into the topic of "From Accra to Seattle (with a Few Detours)"—something I initially underestimated. What began as a routine story evolved into a surprisingly personal audit of where I’ve grown, where I’ve slipped, and what continues to challenge me. I realized that my path hasn't been about linear progress; it’s been a series of weird detours, punchline errors, and the occasional small win that gave me just enough momentum to keep going.

If there's a takeaway, it’s this: context matters. The same challenge that might’ve broken me five years ago now feels like a teachable moment. And maybe that’s the definition of growth. Thanks for sticking with the post—I hope your own journey is full of equally ridiculous, humbling, and surprisingly meaningful moments.

title: The Time I Almost Quit Tech (And Why I’m Glad I Didn’t)
summary: How hitting rock bottom became my career catalyst—and what I tell engineers on the brink.

content.html:
The Breaking Point

February 2018: I was:

  • Debugging a Laravel app for a client who vanished after delivery
  • Burning through savings with 3 months' rent due
  • Facing this error for the 11th hour straight:
    SQLSTATE[HY000] [2002] Connection refused

I remember staring at that error like it was a personal insult. I tried every Stack Overflow answer, restarted MySQL twice, cried once (quietly), and finally just sat in the dark wondering how it all went sideways. I wasn’t new to code—but I was new to the crushing doubt that creeps in when the gigs dry up and the code won’t compile. The impostor syndrome had stopped whispering and started shouting.

What Saved Me

  1. The Pivot: I stopped chasing one-off freelance projects and took a contract role with a startup that actually paid on time. It was less glamorous, but the consistent income let me breathe.
  2. The Mentor: I met a senior dev named Travis (shoutout if you’re reading this). He reviewed one of my GitHub repos and said,
    "Your value isn't in never failing—it's in how you recover."
    That single line reframed how I saw my messy portfolio: not as a graveyard of failed experiments, but as a record of persistence.
  3. The Win: I landed a Shopify developer role by doing something unexpected—I showcased a failed project. In the interview, I walked through the architecture, what broke, what I’d do differently. Turns out, they were more impressed by my ability to reflect than my ability to succeed.

If You're Considering Quitting

If you’ve ever Googled “should I quit tech,” first: breathe. You’re not alone. Most people don’t talk about the valleys—only the mountaintops. But the valleys are where we pick up the grit.

SignHealthy FixWhat I Did
Burnout3-day breakTook a literal hike (Forest Park, Portland)
Skill GapsTargeted learning30 mins daily on Laracasts
IsolationJoin a communityPosted on dev.to, met folks who'd been there
Financial stressStabilize with part-time or contract workTook short gigs at boring companies—it paid off

Rebuilding Confidence

There was no single moment when everything changed. It wasn’t a movie montage. It was a slow climb: small wins, tough lessons, and reframing what "success" looked like. I stopped obsessing over becoming a 10x developer and started aiming to be a 1.2x version of myself—every quarter.

One underrated tip? Teach someone else. I mentored a junior dev who reminded me how far I’d come. When you explain closures to someone just learning loops, you realize: Oh wait—I know things.

What I Tell Engineers On the Brink

  • Quitting is a feeling, not a decision. Let it pass through you. Don’t build a life around it.
  • Find your floor. Not every job needs to be a dream job. Stability is underrated when you’re in survival mode.
  • Build in public—even your failures. That postmortem I wrote? Still my highest-viewed article. Vulnerability is magnetic.
  • Stack Overflow is helpful, but friends who’ll roast you and then send solutions are better.
"Every stuck moment is a future story. Every error message has an expiration date."

Lessons & Reflections

  • The worst part of your career might secretly be the turning point.
  • Consistency outperforms genius when you’re under pressure.
  • Confidence can be rebuilt. But you have to give yourself time—and space—to do it.

title: How I Built MethodistCRM: Laravel, Trials & Triumphs
summary: The church management system that taught me architectural thinking—and how 3AM deployments haunt me.

content.html:
Why Churches Need CRMs Too

The problem: A 200-member congregation tracking donations in Excel, with event RSVPs via WhatsApp. No joke—we once missed a funeral announcement because someone sent the invite to the wrong group chat. I knew we needed structure. My solution stack:

Laravel 5.6
MySQL (with regret)
jQuery (this was 2017, forgive me)

The goal was to centralize communication, donations, and event coordination into one system that felt familiar but functioned far better. The congregation was small, but the feature requests were mighty: SMS reminders, attendance tracking, printable reports, and yes—dark mode. Naturally, I said yes to everything.

Architecture Mistakes → Lessons

This was my first attempt at a full-fledged app with real users (and real consequences). Some of my architectural sins still keep me up at night:

MistakeFixSalesforce Parallel
Monolithic controllersServices patternNow advocate for Lightning Web Components
No testingPHPUnit + CIEnforce 80% coverage at Salesforce
Hardcoded logicConfig files & environment variables12-factor app principles
Direct SQL queries in blade templates 😬Repository patternPlatform events and Apex triggers
"Production outages are the best teachers. Especially when the 'production' is a Sunday service livestream."

The Easter Incident

The app went live a week before Easter. Spirits were high, the choir was rehearsing, and I was on the church Wi-Fi praying my background jobs didn’t break. They broke. Half the congregation couldn’t check in. The donation tracker failed to sync. And the projector displayed a Laravel stack trace instead of the call to worship. A literal `Whoops, something went wrong.` moment—in front of 200 believers.

I spent the next three nights debugging in the sanctuary, occasionally interrupted by choir practice and the odd mosquito. But I fixed it. And I learned that deployment isn't just technical—it's emotional. When people depend on your software in moments that matter, “just reboot it” isn't always an option.

Unexpected Wins

Despite the chaos, something magical happened: people started using it. Pastors loved the insights. Treasurers stopped emailing spreadsheets at 1am. A few younger members even volunteered to help add features. One of them now works in tech. And I realized—this wasn’t just an app. It was a bridge. Between old-school church tradition and modern digital workflows.

I later repurposed parts of the system for other organizations—small nonprofits, a local school, even a food bank. Each time, the core idea remained: build with empathy, not assumptions.

What I’d Do Differently (And What I Wouldn’t)

  • Wouldn’t hardcode anything. Ever. Even the church name was a find/replace away from disaster.
  • Would use migrations and seeding. Manual SQL is a form of penance I no longer practice.
  • Wouldn’t ignore feedback. The best UX advice came from someone who didn’t know how to double-click.
  • Would absolutely do it again. Imperfect code in a real-world context taught me more than any tutorial ever could.

Where It Led Me

That project gave me more than a bullet point on my resume. It gave me language. When I eventually applied at Salesforce, I didn’t talk about abstract skills. I talked about systems built under pressure. I shared that postmortem. I described what it felt like to deploy to a church full of people in their Sunday best. That story resonated more than any HackerRank score ever could.

Even today, when I design something at scale, I think about that tiny print shop and the church CRM. I remember that software is about trust, not just tooling. It’s about anticipating needs, not just shipping features. And it’s about people—messy, wonderful, non-technical people who just want things to work.

Lessons & Reflections

  • Your messy side project might be your clearest case study.
  • Real users are the best QA team you’ll never pay for (and possibly the loudest).
  • Shipping imperfect code into a real-world context will grow you faster than 10 fake projects ever could.

title: My Local Dev Setup: How I Stopped Fighting Docker and Made Peace
summary: From Docker disasters to harmonious containers—a survival guide for full-stack developers.

content.html:
The War of the Ports

When Docker (port 80) declared war on Laravel Valet (also port 80), my development environment became a battlefield. Key casualties:

  • Project A: Laravel app refusing to connect to MySQL
  • Project B: WordPress site showing 'Error establishing database connection'
  • My Sanity: Lost in docker-compose logs output

I was rebooting containers like a caffeinated sysadmin and still couldn’t get `localhost` to behave. One day, I had both Docker and Valet running, and my browser served me a 502 Bad Gateway from the wrong app. It felt like walking into your house and finding a stranger watching Netflix on your couch. Boundaries were being crossed. Ports were being hijacked. It was time to act.

The Peace Treaty

The solution came after hours of trial, error, and a brief spiral into minimalism where I considered building everything in Bash just to avoid Docker entirely. But reason prevailed:

# docker-compose.yml - The Armistice Agreement
version: '3.8'
services:
  app:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
    ports:
      - "${APP_PORT:-8080}:80"  # Compromise: No more port 80 greed
    networks:
      - sail
    volumes:
      - '.:/var/www/html'
networks:
  sail:
    driver: bridge

This tiny change—moving away from port 80—restored peace. Laravel Valet could keep its throne on 80, and Docker could live happily on 8080. I stopped treating my local machine like a zero-sum game and started respecting the boundaries between tools.

Current Stack Allocation

ToolUse CaseWhen to Avoid
DockerMicroservices, team projectsQuick PHP script tests
ValetLegacy projects, local WordPressWhen you need containerization
Node + npm scriptsFrontend builds and hot reloadAPI mocking across services

Other Truces I Had to Negotiate

  • MySQL 8 vs MariaDB: They look alike until you import a dump and everything breaks.
  • Volume mounts on Mac: Slower than molasses if not tuned. I switched to cached mounts and gained back hours of my life.
  • CORS: Not a Docker issue, but it always shows up when you’re already frustrated. Like a parking ticket after a long day.
"The best tool is the one you'll actually use. My setup now looks chaotic but works like a Swiss watch—if Swiss watches occasionally needed docker system prune."

How I Onboard New Projects Now

Every new project starts with a checklist:

  1. Can this run in Valet without side effects? Great. Use Valet.
  2. Need multiple services or team parity? Spin up Docker.
  3. Does it require a custom port? Block it in advance.
  4. Are we exposing 3306 again? Alias it. Always alias it.

I keep a running log of my local ports in a `README-local.md` and document the startup sequence like it’s a NASA launch. Because nothing derails momentum like forgetting that your frontend expects the API on port 5173—but you’re actually running it on 8081 today because your other project refused to shut down properly.

The Bigger Lesson

This whole saga wasn’t really about Docker or Valet. It was about context switching, managing dev fatigue, and accepting that your local machine is not a clean lab environment. It’s a battlefield with layers of tooling piled on like sedimentary rock. And if you don’t pause to make sense of it, eventually you’re knee-deep in logs wondering why `localhost:8000` now returns a WordPress homepage from 2021.

The real upgrade wasn’t just the yml file—it was learning to zoom out. To ask: what does this project need? What do I need to stay productive? Sometimes it’s a bash script. Sometimes it’s a new network alias. Sometimes it’s a deep breath and a walk around the block before you hit ⌘+R one more time.

Lessons & Reflections

  • Don't fight your tools—reconfigure them with empathy for your future self.
  • Write down the weird hacks. You’ll thank yourself a month later.
  • Ports aren’t just numbers—they’re personalities. Some get along. Some absolutely don’t.

title: The 3 Rules I Follow in Code Reviews (and Life)
summary: How giving feedback at Salesforce taught me more about people than programming.

content.html:
Rule #1: Assume Good Intent (Until Proven Otherwise)

At Salesforce, I reviewed a PR where a junior engineer committed node_modules. Instead of "WTF?", I wrote:

"Might want to add node_modules to .gitignore! 
Here's how our team handles dependencies: [link to docs]"

Result: They later told me this kept them from quitting tech. Not because of the technical feedback—but because of the tone. They expected humiliation. They got humanity. That one interaction changed how I review every line of code, and honestly, how I talk to people outside GitHub too.

Rule #2: Be Specific, Not Sarcastic

Sarcasm is the easiest fallback when you're tired, frustrated, or trying to prove how much more you know. But it's lazy communication. Precision is the real flex. I once left a comment that just said, “Interesting approach.” The author didn’t know if I meant it as praise or critique. I had to DM and clarify it was genuine. Lesson: if your feedback can be misinterpreted, it will be.

Now I say things like, “I haven’t seen this pattern used before—can you walk me through the tradeoffs?” or “Would love to understand your thought process here, especially around performance.” You still challenge the code—but not the coder.

Rule #3: Balance Critique With Curiosity

The best code reviews I’ve received didn’t just tell me what was wrong. They asked what I was trying to do. They left space for a dialogue. That curiosity made me feel seen—and helped uncover use cases I hadn’t considered.

So now I leave comments like:

  • “This works, but I wonder—how does it handle edge case X?”
  • “What happens if the API call fails here? Worth wrapping in a try/catch?”
  • “How do you feel about moving this logic into a reusable hook/service?”

It’s not about softening the message. It’s about sharpening the impact by making it a two-way street.

The Framework

SituationBad ResponseBetter Approach
Messy code"This is unreadable""Could we break this into smaller functions?"
Buggy logic"This won't work""What edge cases should we consider?"
Unclear naming"Terrible var name""Could we rename this for clarity around its purpose?"
"A code review is a conversation, not a court ruling. The best feedback I've given started with 'What if...' instead of 'Don't...'"

Bonus: Reviews Aren’t Just For Code

I’ve started applying these same rules in life. When my kid spills something after I just cleaned the kitchen, I pause before reacting. When a teammate misses a meeting, I check in instead of jumping to conclusions. The principles scale. Assume good intent. Be specific. Stay curious.

Feedback is one of the most human things we do at work—and one of the most overlooked skills to master. And like code, it can be refactored over time. You’ll get better with practice.

What I Wish I’d Known Sooner

  • Public humiliation doesn’t teach as well as private encouragement.
  • Junior engineers remember how you made them feel more than what you said.
  • Your tone in PRs can either nurture a team or quietly corrode it.
  • Reviews are opportunities to teach, learn, and model culture—not just ship code.

Lessons & Reflections

  • Code reviews are emotional terrain. Tread with care, not caution.
  • The best engineers I’ve worked with are the best communicators—especially in critique.
  • Compassion scales better than cleverness.

title: What Working at Salesforce Taught Me About Scaling Myself
summary: From solo developer to team multiplier—lessons in working at enterprise scale.

content.html:
The Tableau Marketing Engineering Playbook

Three scaling strategies I now swear by:

  1. Documentation as Force Multiplier: My onboarding.md has saved 37+ engineer-hours. It started as a personal “reminder log” and became the most cloned doc on our internal Confluence. I included things like how to run tests, edge case notes, known quirks of our GA integration, and even Slack etiquette. Now, new hires ping me to say, “That doc saved me two days.”
  2. The 30% Rule: Spend 30% of sprint capacity on tech debt—or pay 300% later. I’ve lived both sides. At one point, we deferred one too many refactors and ended up rebuilding a component mid-quarter while trying to ship two campaigns. Chaos. Now, tech debt is budgeted like a utility bill—non-negotiable.
  3. PR Templates: Standardized formats cut review time by 40%. I added sections for context, test cases, screenshots, and rollback plans. It felt silly at first, but it eliminated 80% of the “can you explain this?” comments. And reviewers now leave comments like, “Nice context. LGTM.” Which is basically love in PR language.

Before/After Salesforce

MetricPre-SalesforceNow
Code Reviews/Day1-28-10 (with higher quality)
Meeting Efficiency"Let's discuss"Pre-circulated Loom videos
Reusability of Components"Copy/paste with tweaks"Published as internal packages

Team Impact as a Metric

I used to measure my productivity by commits and tickets closed. Now I track something fuzzier but more powerful: how many people I’ve unblocked, how often my solutions get reused, and whether the team runs smoother when I’m not around. That last one used to scare me. Now I see it as the goal.

One month, I took a staycation and came back to find teammates had used my docs, scripts, and templates to deploy three updates. I had a mini identity crisis—was I still needed? The answer, of course, was yes. But in a different way. Less keyboard hero. More systems gardener.

"At scale, your keyboard skills matter less than your ability to make others 10% better. I measure my impact in GitHub forks now."

How I Think About Scaling Now

Scaling yourself isn’t just delegation. It’s clarity, context, and removing friction for others. It’s asking “Will this break if I disappear for a week?” and building accordingly. That might mean writing better internal docs. Or automating a routine process. Or creating a team glossary because nobody knows what 'chassis' means anymore.

I’ve also learned to give context upfront—in PRs, Jira tickets, Slack threads—so teammates don’t have to dig. I think of it like future-proofing empathy. If someone’s having a rough week, can my message help them without draining more energy? Can they say “ah, got it” without needing to call a meeting? That’s the bar.

What Scaling Myself Didn’t Mean

  • Working more hours: In fact, I started protecting deep work time more aggressively.
  • Becoming a manager: Scaling doesn’t require a title change. Influence is scale.
  • Automating everything: Some things (like onboarding coffee chats) are better human.

Little Systems, Big Impact

Here are a few micro-systems I’ve set up that made a disproportionate difference:

  • A one-click script that sets up local dev for our GA4 pipeline. Saved at least five onboarding sessions.
  • A Slack alias @ga4-help that routes questions to a rotating support dev. No more silent suffering or Slack DMs at 11pm.
  • A calendar block called "Maker Mornings"—three no-meeting hours daily. I evangelized it, now half the team does it.

Lessons & Reflections

  • If it’s painful now, someone else will feel it worse later. Fix it early, or document it honestly.
  • You don’t scale by doing more. You scale by enabling more.
  • Good systems are invisible when they work and unforgettable when they don’t.

title: Debugging, Parenting, and Other High-Stakes Fire Drills
summary: Why troubleshooting production issues prepared me for toddler meltdowns.

content.html:
Parallels Between Code and Kids

Debugging TacticParenting Application
Check recent changes"What did you eat before this tantrum?"
Isolate variables"Is it the socks or the shoes bothering you?"
Roll back last deployment"Let's go back to bedtime routine version 1.3"
Logs & ObservabilityAsk your partner, who was watching five minutes ago

Parenting and production debugging have more overlap than I ever expected. Both involve unpredictable systems, unclear documentation, and stakeholders who will absolutely scream if you break something.

Critical Tools for Both

# Parenting Stack
1. Snack Break         # Equivalent to restarting the server
2. Distraction Tactic  # Like rolling back a deployment
3. Sleep Debugging     # Works on toddlers AND Kubernetes
4. Incident Report     # AKA "What did we learn from that LEGO mishap?"
"The only difference between a midnight diaper change and a PagerDuty alert? One lets you claim overtime."

When Both Worlds Collide

There was a night when the production API failed right as my daughter spilled applesauce on the TV remote. I had one hand on a laptop, the other wiping a sticky screen, and a toddler yelling, “WHY IS COCOMELON GONE?” It was the most stressful failover scenario I’ve ever managed.

That’s when it hit me: parenting trained me to stay calm under fire. It’s just that in one world the logs are JSON, and in the other, they're crayon drawings on the wall.

Incident Response IRL

When a production bug takes down a service, we rally, diagnose, and fix fast. But at home, the incident response might involve three rounds of negotiation, bribery via popsicles, and ultimately a forced restart (read: nap).

One of my kids once refused to wear anything but a superhero cape for a week. No shirt, no shoes—just the cape. After trying logic, persuasion, and pleading, I gave in and documented it as a Known Issue. Sometimes you don’t fix the bug—you just contain it and move on.

Systems Thinking Everywhere

As a dev, I think in inputs, outputs, and failure modes. Now I’ve started applying the same mindset to the bedtime routine:

  • Inputs: Tooth brushing, story time, last sip of water
  • Output: Asleep child
  • Failure Modes: Too much sugar, scary story, missing blanket

I’ve literally created flowcharts for our morning routine. My spouse thinks I’m ridiculous. But we haven’t missed the school bus in six months.

What Parenting Has Taught Me About Tech (and Vice Versa)

  • Don’t assume the problem is obvious—ask better questions.
  • Clear communication matters more than clever solutions.
  • Sometimes the fix isn’t elegant—it’s duct tape and a promise to revisit it next week.
  • Resilience beats perfection. The system (or the child) will crash. Your job is to recover quickly and kindly.

My Favorite Multi-Domain Debugging Wins

  • The Nighttime Downtime: When a toddler wakes up at 2am screaming, check: dry diaper, water level, blanket alignment. If all else fails, cuddle. (Analogous to restarting Redis.)
  • The API Timeout: When a child stares blankly and doesn’t respond, assume buffer overload. Try gentle prompts. If no response, offer snack (or `curl -I localhost:snack`).
  • The Pull Request Review: When a kid proudly shows you their block tower and it’s leaning like Pisa, say: “Nice start! Want to add support at the base?” Works every time.

Lessons & Reflections

  • The best debugging isn’t about fixing fast—it’s about understanding deeply.
  • Systems—whether digital or human—are messy, emotional, and non-linear.
  • Patience, presence, and perspective are your best tools, whether you’re handling a 500 error or a five-year-old meltdown.

title: My Favorite Tech Snacks, Ranked by Debugging Productivity
summary: A scientific(ly dubious) analysis of snack-based problem-solving.

content.html:
The Snack Debugging Matrix

SnackBest ForProductivity Boost
Dark ChocolateArchitecture problems+42% focus (measured by commits/hour)
Gummy BearsCSS battles+27% patience for Safari bugs
Mixed NutsCI/CD pipeline flakinessModerate stress tolerance, +1 GitHub Copilot accuracy
Spicy Plantain ChipsRegex hellFire in both the syntax and your mouth

The Fatal Mistake

Never attempt:

Doritos + Keyboard == 💻🔥
# True story: Required 3 isopropyl wipes

Let’s just say the crunch-to-keystroke ratio was not in my favor. Learned the hard way that dust + mechanical switches = sad ticket updates.

"A well-timed snack break is like GC for your brain. My record? Solved a Docker networking issue during a peanut butter cracker intermission."

The Snack-to-Stack Matching Theory

Over the years, I’ve developed a working theory: every technical problem has a snack that matches its intensity and mood. This is not scientific—but it is battle-tested.

  • Node module version mismatches? Sour candy. Because your soul is already sour.
  • Legacy PHP refactoring? Rice crackers. Low reward, high crunch. Keeps you awake.
  • Last-minute deploy to production on Friday? Something handheld and prayer-friendly. I recommend almonds.

There's something incredibly grounding about chewing while stepping through logs. It slows the panic. Gives you time to think. Or at least to stall while you Google “what does this stack trace mean.”

Snack Budgeting: The DevOps Edition

I once built a CI notification Slack bot that triggered a “snack time” reminder if three consecutive deploys failed. It felt like a joke—until the team started using it. Someone even added custom reactions: 🧃 for juice, 🥨 for pretzels, 🍫 for emergencies.

We didn’t fix the pipeline immediately, but we laughed. And that lowered cortisol more effectively than another retro ever could.

Snack Drawer Observability

Every senior engineer has a mental model of their local setup, their AWS permissions, and their snack drawer hierarchy. Mine is organized by failure type:

  • Top left: Debug snacks (dark chocolate, apple slices, brain fuel)
  • Bottom drawer: Post-deploy victory stash (mini Snickers, gummy worms)
  • Emergency bin: Mints, instant coffee packs, and… a single fortune cookie from 2019 labeled “Do Not Open Unless Build Fails”

Snack-Based Pair Programming Tips

Remote pair programming changed everything—except my commitment to mid-call snack rituals. Here’s what works:

  • Before sharing screen: Munch something crunchy to clear your head. (Mute, obviously.)
  • During review: Go soft—chewy granola or banana. Keeps energy up, doesn’t distract.
  • If the PR is cursed: One bite of dark chocolate per commit. Set limits. (Or don’t.)

Also: if your pair brings snacks too, you know it's a good match. One guy I worked with used to code with trail mix and heavy jazz. Together we fixed an OAuth bug and gained three pounds.

The Snack Stack That Broke Me

Worst combo ever attempted: espresso beans + jalapeño chips + frontend state management rewrite. I don’t remember what I shipped, but I do remember it came with a two-day migraine and an apology commit.

Lessons & Reflections

  • Small comforts (like snacks) create psychological safety during high-pressure work.
  • Debugging is easier with a pause button—snacks are a great excuse to step back.
  • Never eat powdered snacks while touching a MacBook. That’s not even a metaphor. Just don’t.

Why This Still Matters

My Favorite Tech Snacks, Ranked by Debugging Productivity wasn’t just an episode—it was a turning point. The details may fade, but the lessons endure.

  • Small wins build confidence that snowballs.
  • Failures are more educational than tutorials.
  • Community—mentors, blog readers, Stack Overflow warriors—makes the difference.

Closing Thoughts

If you're early in your journey: keep going. If you're seasoned: share more. The ecosystem thrives when we all document the messy, real, and remarkable stories that shape us. And if you take nothing else away from this post, remember: it's okay to snack during deployment.

title: Why I Still Love PHP (Even After All These Years)
summary: In defense of the internet's most-maligned language—and why Laravel changed everything.

content.html:
PHP's Unfair Reputation

Modern PHP vs. the stereotypes:

Criticism2024 Reality
"Inconsistent functions"Framework wrappers (Laravel's Str, Arr)
"Slow"PHP 8.3 benchmarks faster than Node
"Ugly syntax"Blade templates are cleaner than most JSX

Where PHP Still Shines

// Laravel's elegance in one snippet
Route::get('/posts', [PostController::class, 'index']);

// vs. the old way
if ($_SERVER['REQUEST_URI'] == '/posts') {
  $posts = mysql_query('SELECT * FROM posts');
  include('templates/posts.php');
}

I’ve written JavaScript, Python, even some Rust. But when I need to ship fast and build something for real people, PHP is still the tool I reach for—especially with Laravel smoothing out the edges. It’s like meeting an old friend who’s now wearing tailored suits and talking about container orchestration.

"PHP is like Accra's tro-tros—messy but gets millions where they need to go. Laravel is the air-conditioned VIP bus version."

The Evolution Nobody Talks About

PHP was the wild west back in the day. Inline HTML, spaghetti code, global variables like party crashers. But the community matured. Composer happened. PSRs brought standards. Frameworks emerged. Laravel gave us syntactic joy. Symfony brought enterprise confidence. PHPUnit made tests not only possible but elegant. And the tooling? Way better than people give it credit for.

Every time someone says, “Wait, you still use PHP?” I just smile. Then I show them Horizon, Vapor, Tinker, and a zero-downtime deployment pipeline. That usually changes the tone of the conversation.

Why I Still Reach for PHP

  • Community: Laravel's ecosystem is opinionated—in a good way. I rarely have to reinvent wheels. I just build.
  • Hosting: You can deploy a Laravel app on a $5 VPS, a Heroku clone, or a Kubernetes cluster. It doesn’t care.
  • Speed to Value: I can spin up a CRUD interface in 15 minutes. And it's not just fast—it feels right.
  • Battle-tested: PHP has powered the web for two decades. It’s not glamorous, but it works. And keeps working.

How Laravel Changed the Game

Laravel was a turning point. Suddenly, PHP had expressive routing, Eloquent ORM, Blade templates, and artisan commands that felt like magic. For devs who grew up on CodeIgniter or raw PHP, it was like jumping from a bicycle to a Tesla.

Laravel turned PHP from a tool you tolerated into a tool you admired. It gave us confidence that we could write clean, modern, testable code—and still deploy fast.

The Sentimental Side

PHP is the language that taught me to code. It powered my first freelance gig. It paid my rent when I was starting out. My first Stripe integration, my first major bug, my first 3am deployment—all PHP. So yeah, I’m biased. But that bias is earned. Through repetition, repair, and relentless Googling.

Even today, when I crack open a `.env` file and see `DB_CONNECTION=mysql`, I get a little nostalgic. This was the stack that built my confidence and gave me permission to call myself a developer.

Things I’ve Built With PHP (And Still Would)

  • Church CRMs
  • Blog engines
  • Booking systems
  • Intranet portals for teams that didn’t know what an API was
  • WordPress hacks that somehow still run today

Would I reach for Node or Python in some cases now? Sure. But if the client needs a backend with speed, reliability, and proven plugins for payments, queues, file uploads, and email? I’m going Laravel every time.

Lessons & Reflections

  • Don’t dismiss a language just because it was mocked in a 2010 Hacker News thread.
  • The best tools are the ones that make you feel capable—regardless of trends.
  • Clean code is more about discipline than syntax. PHP lets you be messy, but also rewards you for being thoughtful.

Why This Still Matters

Why I Still Love PHP (Even After All These Years) wasn’t just an episode—it was a turning point. The details may fade, but the lessons endure.

  • Small wins build confidence that snowballs.
  • Failures are more educational than tutorials.
  • Community—mentors, blog readers, Stack Overflow warriors—makes the difference.

Closing Thoughts

If you're early in your journey: keep going. If you're seasoned: share more. The ecosystem thrives when we all document the messy, real, and remarkable stories that shape us. And if you take nothing else away from this post, remember: it's okay to snack during deployment.

title: How I Prepared for My Salesforce Interview
summary: The exact study plan that helped me transition from freelancer to FAANG+ engineer.

content.html:
The 6-Week Preparation Blueprint

  1. Business Acumen: Memorized Tableau's GTM strategy. I didn’t just study the company—I tried to speak its language. I browsed earnings reports, read product updates, and watched Dreamforce keynotes. I wanted to be able to answer, “Why Salesforce?” without sounding generic.
  2. System Design: Practiced with Salesforce Architecture Cases. I built mock diagrams on a whiteboard in my basement and ran through them out loud. My wife thought I was arguing with myself. I was. About horizontal scaling.
  3. Behavioral: Scripted 15 STAR stories. Real ones—about client meltdowns, 3am outages, and mentoring junior devs through their first PRs. I rehearsed until the nerves turned into rhythm.

Interview Day Cheat Sheet

StageMy Strategy
CodingVerbally confirmed constraints first. Asked clarifying questions even if I was 90% sure—because it showed I cared about requirements, not just algorithms.
System DesignDrew parallels to MethodistCRM. Walked them through architecture trade-offs I'd made in real life. Used latency numbers and traffic assumptions grounded in my own past experience.
BehavioralConnected past challenges to the Salesforce culture. Showed not just what I did, but how I think and grow.
"They don't expect you to know everything—just how to learn anything. I cited debugging the print shop's cash register as my first 'system.'"

What I Did Differently

Instead of grinding LeetCode endlessly, I spent focused time on:

  • Mock interviews with friends (even ones who weren’t in tech)
  • Whiteboarding non-trivial past projects like they were system design prompts
  • Pairing with a mentor once a week to simulate peer code reviews and rapid feedback

I also wrote out my tech “origin story”—not for them, but for me. It reminded me why I cared. That turned my nerves into purpose. When the call came, I didn’t feel like I was performing. I felt like I was inviting someone into my world.

The Curveballs

Not everything went to plan. In one round, I froze halfway through a recursive function. Total blank. I took a breath, laughed, and said, “This is a mental stack overflow—mind if I talk it out?” The interviewer smiled. We debugged my thought process together. And I finished strong.

Another time, I misunderstood a behavioral question. I paused, asked if I could reframe, and gave a better example. The grace wasn’t in knowing the answer—it was in recovering transparently. I think they valued that more than any flawless pitch.

What Helped the Most

  • Sleep. Seriously. I stopped cramming after 10pm. Clear thinking > more practice.
  • Practicing storytelling. Interviews are data, yes—but they’re also narrative. You’re showing who you are through how you explain.
  • Creating a mock interviewer guide. I gave friends a doc with sample questions, signals to watch for, and space to write feedback.

Post-Interview Reflection

I didn’t walk away from the interviews thinking “I nailed that.” I walked away thinking “I represented myself clearly.” That was the win. If they said no, I knew I’d still grown from the process. That mindset kept me grounded.

A week later, the offer came. And I didn’t celebrate with champagne—I celebrated with rest. Because preparing for a job at this level isn’t just about readiness. It’s about sustainability. It’s about pacing your growth so you don’t burn out before you begin.

Lessons & Reflections

  • You don’t need to be perfect. You need to be present, prepared, and real.
  • Translate your past, don’t minimize it. Your odd side projects might be your secret strength.
  • Preparation is more than drills—it’s self-awareness, clarity, and control under pressure.

title: Docker Networking for Humans: A Simplified Guide
summary: How I finally understood containers talking to each other—without a networking degree.

content.html:
The Breakthrough Moment

When I realized Docker networking is just:

containers as apartments
networks as streets
ports as mailboxes

That analogy unlocked everything. Once I stopped thinking in IP addresses and started thinking in city planning, container networking finally clicked. Each container is its own unit with its own address. Networks connect them like city roads. Ports? Just the mailboxes at the curb. No need to memorize—just map it visually.

Real-World Comms Examples

NeedSolution
Laravel → MySQLSame custom network
Vue → APIPublished ports + CORS
WordPress → MariaDBDocker Compose + named volumes + service linking
phpMyAdmin accessExpose to host via localhost:8081

Once you name your networks and align services on the same one, you stop having to guess why localhost works in your browser but not inside a container. (Spoiler: it’s never really localhost unless you're the host.)

"Troubleshooting tip: docker network inspect is your Google Maps for container traffic. My 'eureka' moment came when I named networks after Accra neighborhoods."

From “Works on My Machine” to “Works for the Team”

My first Docker-based team project was chaos. Containers couldn’t find each other, exposed ports clashed with local Valet, and every teammate had a different solution. Eventually, we created a dedicated network called team-net, standardized our docker-compose.yml files, and documented our internal service names.

Magically, things stabilized. Laravel could find MySQL by name (mysql), Vue could call api:8000, and nobody had to ask “what port is Postgres using again?” for the hundredth time.

Docker DNS Is Underrated

Most people don’t realize Docker sets up its own DNS when you use custom networks. So instead of IPs, just use service names. Want your app container to talk to the MySQL container? Just point it to mysql. Want to ping Redis? Use redis. No static IPs. No hacks. Just... names.

It's like magic, but actually just engineering.

Debugging Networking Issues Without Losing Your Mind

  • Start with docker network ls — make sure your containers are on the same network
  • Use docker exec and ping — check if containers can talk to each other
  • Try curl service:port — to confirm exposed interfaces work internally
  • Use docker-compose ps — and verify names and exposed ports

Also: when in doubt, restart everything. Containers get salty. It’s not you. It’s the layer-2 bridge driver being moody again.

The Quick Mental Model I Teach Now

  • Browser ↔ Host: Uses localhost:port
  • Container ↔ Container: Uses service name on same network
  • Container ↔ Internet: Needs proper EXPOSE and port forwarding

I used to draw complicated diagrams. Now I just say: “Pretend it’s an apartment building. The hallways are networks. If they’re on the same hallway, they can talk. If not, use the front desk (host) to connect them.”

Bonus: Docker Compose Tips That Save You Time

  • Always name your networks in docker-compose.yml—and reuse them
  • Use depends_on for sequencing but not for health checks
  • Add healthcheck blocks so containers wait before throwing errors
  • For frontend → backend calls, document your internal vs. external URLs

And don’t forget to alias your API hostnames when testing in the browser. Inside the container, api:8000. Outside? localhost:8000. Know the difference.

Lessons & Reflections

  • Networking isn’t scary when you stop chasing IPs and start thinking in metaphors.
  • Most Docker bugs are just mismatched assumptions between host, container, and browser.
  • Documentation is your friend. Draw diagrams. Annotate your compose files. Share them.

title: This Meeting Could’ve Been a Comment (But It Wasn’t)
summary: How I reduced my meeting load by 70%—without becoming 'that guy.'

content.html:
The Async Communication Stack

My tiered approach to avoiding meetings:

if (problem.complexity < 2) {
  return 'Slack thread';
} else if (context.needed) {
  return 'Loom video';
} else {
  return 'Calendar invite';
}

This flow has saved me—and my team—dozens of hours each sprint. It’s not about being antisocial. It’s about clarity, autonomy, and letting people actually do their work without turning every decision into a video call with 9 attendees and 0 conclusions.

When Meetings Are Actually Needed

Meeting TypeMy Rules
StandupsAlways async on Fridays
RetrosPre-filled board required
1:1sOnly when we have something meaningful to reflect on—not just to "check in"
Design ReviewsDeck or doc circulated 24 hours in advance

I’m not anti-meeting. I’m pro-purpose. The best meetings I’ve had felt like code reviews: scoped, specific, and designed to ship something—an idea, a resolution, a next step. Everything else is cargo cult collaboration.

"A good meeting is like a good pull request—clear purpose, minimal noise, and actionable outcomes. Bonus points if no one says 'circle back.'"

How I Made the Shift

I used to accept every invite like it was a royal summons. 30 minutes here, 45 there—suddenly half my day was gone. I wasn’t getting deep work done. I wasn’t solving problems. I was talking about maybe solving problems later. So I tried something radical: I started saying no. Or at least, “Can we async this?”

At first, it felt risky—like I was breaking a secret social contract. But then people started thanking me. They got time back too. One engineer told me my Loom videos were the only meetings he could play at 2x speed and still get value.

Async Culture Isn’t Lazy—It’s Respectful

When I record a Loom, I make sure it’s tight, organized, and intentional. I even include chapter markers sometimes. Why? Because people deserve context without the obligation of synchronous presence. Async isn’t lower effort. Done right, it’s higher empathy.

And when someone replies with a thoughtful comment? Instant serotonin. Fewer meetings. Better ideas. More trust.

How I Train Teams to Communicate Better

  • Default to written proposals: If you can’t explain it in a page, it’s not meeting-ready.
  • Record short updates: A 4-minute video beats a 30-minute call. Every time.
  • Keep Slack threads structured: Use threads, emojis for voting, and summaries after decisions.
  • Document the why, not just the what: Future-you (or your teammates) will thank you.

The Exceptions That Prove the Rule

Of course, some meetings matter:

  • Conflict resolution? Synchronous, always.
  • Big launches or retros with emotion baked in? Real-time helps.
  • 1:1s with direct reports? Use that space for reflection, feedback, and growth—not status updates.

But when a “quick sync” becomes a default habit instead of an intentional tool, you're stealing time—and usually replacing clarity with noise.

Slack Isn’t Always Async Either

Let’s be clear: Slack can become just as noisy as Zoom. Pings ≠ progress. If you’re responding to DMs all day, you’re not async—you’re just always on. True async means establishing response windows, letting people batch their focus, and not expecting answers within 10 minutes unless there’s 🚒 in the subject line.

Lessons & Reflections

  • Every meeting should have a purpose, a plan, and a path forward.
  • Async-first doesn’t mean no meetings—it means better ones.
  • The real cost of meetings isn’t time—it’s context switching.
